All rights reserved. Big Ten Wrestling A World Champion, A New Style: Masanosuke Ono Ready For Penn State
 World champion Masanosuke Ono prepares for his Penn State debut after adapting to a new language, culture and wrestling style.
 Nov 11, 2026 By Travis Johnson • 4 min read News Folkstyle College Division I Men NCAA Big Ten Pennsylvania Penn State Penn State Men's Wrestling Men's Wrestling Big Ten Big Ten Wrestling Masanosuke Ono Masanosuke Ono didn’t wrestle a single match for Penn State last season, but the Japanese phenom still made a massive first impression in Happy Valley.
 Now, the freestyle World champion is ready to make his college debut.
 Ono is expected to wrestle at 133 pounds Thursday when the Nittany Lions open their season against Bloomsburg. It’ll be a welcome milestone in Ono’s journey that’s seen him venture nearly 6,800 miles from home, adapt to an unfamiliar culture, overcome a nagging health issue and get up to speed on a new language and wrestling style in less than 20 months.
 “I think it just shows his desire and his passion and his willingness to work,” Penn State coach Cael Sanderson said. “He wants to be an NCAA champion. That’s his goal. Of course, there’s incredible wrestlers at every weight in the NCAA, but I think the biggest challenge for him to start was the language barrier and being able to pass his classes. There’s just no way you can take shortcuts in there, and he didn’t.”
 Ono, who won gold in the 2024 World Championships at 61 kilograms, is listed as a senior on Penn State’s roster that was released this week. He’s studying philosophy, getting As and has quickly picked up English by working with an interpreter, Sanderson said.
 He’s also developed as a folkstyle prospect.
 Ono notched a 4-0 win over NCAA runner-up Ben Davino in a Real American Freestyle event in August. After the match, Ono gave his first on-camera interview of the season to Nittany Sports Now.
 Still sweaty from his scuffle with the Buckeye star, Ono admitted that picking up the nuances of folkstyle had been “very difficult” and said many of his teammates were able to take him down consistently.
 That might sound preposterous to anyone who watched Ono outscore his opponents 55-2 at the 2024 World Championships with wins over World champions Vito Arujau and Zaur Uguev. 
 Sanderson glanced up at the neon lights in Rec Hall on Tuesday as if he was trying to remember Ono being taken down with any regularity in the Penn State room.
 He offered a wry smile to downplay Ono’s own self-assessment.
 “He can wrestle folkstyle,” Sanderson said. “I don’t see him get taken down too much and he’s wrestling really, really good guys, obviously. But he’s a very humble guy and very coachable, just very grateful. He’s very like-minded. Fits in our program really well.”
 And with All-American Marcus Blaze moving up to 141 pounds, Ono should be a perfect fit in the team’s lineup.
 It’s a weight that works for the compact, broad-shouldered Ono. Having won his World title at its equivalent 61 kilograms, Ono attempted to cut to 57 kilograms for Japan’s Emperor’s Cup last December. He had to withdraw due to dehydration issues related to the cut, however.
 His recovery delayed his folkstyle training and Sanderson routinely was asked last season as Penn State chased its 15th NCAA title if Ono would contribute.
 Now, the time is here.
 Rocco Welsh can identify with Ono. Both were among the team’s “new guys” a year ago.
 Welsh, a Pennsylvania native, returned to his home state from Ohio State. He admitted then that making the transition was awkward at first. He knows Ono’s took an even bigger chance getting even further outside of his comfort zone.
 “He probably had everything made in Japan, being a World champion, young, his whole family is there,” Welsh said. “It’s pretty impressive what he’s done. Moving here, learning a new language. I don’t think he has a driver’s license or anything really, so everything’s different and he’s just doing it.”
 Welsh’s Focus 
 Welsh, who has five career falls, admitted he’s “never really been a big pinner.”
 That could change this season.
 The 184-pound NCAA runner-up said he spent a lot of time in the offseason working on developing his offense from the top and quick transitions from takedowns to turns.  
 “Yeah, I’m looking to pin some people for sure,” Welsh said.
 He’s also looking to teammate Mitchell Mesenbrink for more inspiration. Ironically, Mesenbrink was the first Penn State wrestler Welsh drilled with when he transferred from Ohio State last year.
 Their size differential made it tough for them to regularly go with one another, however. Now, with Mesenbrink up at 174 pounds, Welsh plans to seek him out for more sparring sessions in practice.
 Mesenbrink’s method also serves as a proof of concept for what Welsh wants to do. The Hodge Trophy winner won his first NCAA title in 2025 with zero pins all season. A year later Mesenbrink notched a career-best eight falls en route to his second NCAA title. 
 “I really think it’s mainly his mindset,” Welsh said. “Everybody knows how to shoot and snap people down and sprawl and stuff, I really think it’s pretty impressive what he can do. He just turns his mind off and goes. No fear or nothing. Just faith. That’s what I’m trying to do.”
 Waiting Game
 Having recently returned from the World Championships where he won bronze at 61 kilograms, Blaze will wait to make his debut up a weight at 141.
 In the meantime, the Nittany Lions can fill the spot with one of a handful of capable wrestlers.
 Two interesting options? Do-it-all sophomore Nate Desmond and talented freshman Sam Herring.
 Herring is likely out for now as he spent most of the last month as Zain Retherford’s training partner as Retherford competed in the World Championships. Sanderson said the freshman PIAA placewinner was a bit behind in folkstyle preparation.
 Desmond, meanwhile, is looking to build on a strong freshman season that saw him fill in at multiple points throughout the lineup. He wrestled at 125 and 141 and went 7-0 with three bonus-point wins.
 “Desmond has shown he can wrestle any weight,” Sanderson said. “He’s just a beast all the way around.”
